# The prelude: typed declarations of the language's built-in functions (`len`, `to_s`, ...). The resolver admits
# this unit into every program, the way Rust and Swift load their preludes, so a builtin call's types come from a
# declaration here rather than from a table of names. Name resolution is unchanged: a user definition with the same
# name shadows a builtin by the ordinary scope rules, and a call the resolver classifies as a builtin carries the
# runtime identity it selected; HIR joins that identity to the declaration below that links to it.
#
# Every builtin belongs to a namespace: the module that declares it here (Text.find, Env.get). The qualified
# reference is what is reserved; a user name never conflicts with it. `implicit` marks the small core set every
# program sees bare; a user definition that changes what a bare call to one of those resolves to gets a warning.
# `role` names the language operation a builtin performs (place_update, place_read), so the compiler finds it by
# role, never by name. The `## ` doc comment above each declaration is its one-line summary, which
# `hey doc --reserved` lists.
#
# This file is Hey's internal extern bindings: INTERNAL-ONLY. Programs reach its namespaces (Text.find, Env.get) as
# builtins; only a file under stdlib/ may import this file by path (the resolver refuses any other file).
# `extern`, `implicit` and `role` are internal (stdlib/runtime_bindings/ only). Each extern line names the runtime
# callable it binds. A builtin with more than one arity is an ordinary function here, `implicit fn`, with an optional
# parameter; it calls one single-arity internal binding per arity (HeyRuntimeBindings), never an extern overload
# (coordinator ruling 2026-10-29). A bare call that no definition of the program answers resolves to it.
#
# A parameter borrows its argument unless it says otherwise: `update` means the runtime callable may change the
# argument in place when the caller holds the only reference (the caller rebinds the result, as in
# `set m = put(m, k, v)`), and `consume` means the callable takes the argument over. MIR reads these as the
# ownership facts of the call.
import 'stdlib:runtime_bindings/HeyRuntimeBindings'
import 'stdlib:runtime_bindings/HeyCompilerIntrinsics'

module Core
  ## The length of a list, record, map or string.
  implicit extern fn len(value: Value) -> Int = BuiltIns len
  ## The value written as text.

  ## The name of the value's runtime type.
  implicit extern fn type(value: Value) -> String = BuiltIns type
  ## Whether a record or map holds the key, or a list holds the element.

  ## The value stored under key in a record or map, or at an index of a list.

  ## A copy of the container with key set to value.
  implicit role place_update extern fn put(update container: Value, key: Value, value: Value) -> Value = BuiltIns put
  ## A copy of the list with the value added at the end.

  ## The value written as JSON text (as Json.encode). Declared here: Json.encode names another runtime callable.

  ## Internal strict binding; programs write Text.parse_int.
  extern fn parse_int(text: Value) -> Int = BuiltIns parse_int
  ## The integer a value converts to; with a base (2 to 36, or 0 to read a 0x, 0o or 0b prefix), the integer the text spells.
  implicit fn to_i(value: Value, base: Value = nil) -> Int
    if base == nil
      return HeyRuntimeBindings.to_i_value(value)
    end
    return HeyRuntimeBindings.to_i_base(value, base)
  end

  implicit fn Int(value: Value, base: Value = nil) -> Int
    if base == nil

  end
  ## The bytes of a value; with an encoding (utf-8 or ascii), the text encoded in it.

    if encoding == nil
      return HeyRuntimeBindings.bytes_value(value)

  end
  ## The text of a value; with an encoding (utf-8 or ascii), the bytes decoded from it.

    if encoding == nil

    return HeyRuntimeBindings.text_decoded(value, encoding)

    return HeyRuntimeBindings.io_file(path, mode)

# The prelude: typed declarations of the language's built-in functions (`len`, `to_s`, ...). The resolver admits
# this unit into every program, the way Rust and Swift load their preludes, so a builtin call's types come from a
# declaration here rather than from a table of names. Name resolution is unchanged: a user definition with the same
# name shadows a builtin by the ordinary scope rules, and a call the resolver classifies as a builtin carries the
# runtime identity it selected; HIR joins that identity to the declaration below that links to it.
#
# Every builtin belongs to a namespace: the module that declares it here (Text.find, Env.get). The qualified
# reference is what is reserved; a user name never conflicts with it. `implicit` marks the small core set every
# program sees bare; a user definition that changes what a bare call to one of those resolves to gets a warning.
# `role` names the language operation a builtin performs (place_update, place_read), so the compiler finds it by
# role, never by name. The `## ` doc comment above each declaration is its one-line summary, which
# `hey doc --reserved` lists.
#
# This file is Hey's internal extern bindings: INTERNAL-ONLY. Programs reach its namespaces (Text.find, Env.get) as
# builtins; only a file under stdlib/ may import this file by path (the resolver refuses any other file).
# `extern`, `implicit` and `role` are internal (stdlib/runtime_bindings/ only). Each extern line names the runtime
# callable it binds. A builtin with more than one arity is an ordinary function here, `implicit fn`, with an optional
# parameter; it calls one single-arity internal binding per arity (HeyRuntimeBindings), never an extern overload
# (coordinator ruling 2026-10-29). A bare call that no definition of the program answers resolves to it.
#
# A parameter borrows its argument unless it says otherwise: `update` means the runtime callable may change the
# argument in place when the caller holds the only reference (the caller rebinds the result, as in
# `set m = put(m, k, v)`), and `consume` means the callable takes the argument over. MIR reads these as the
# ownership facts of the call.
